analysis.one_liner: Caps oil company wholesale profits and gas price hikes, and orders a price-gouging probe after Katrina.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced days after Hurricane Katrina sent gas prices soaring, never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Energy Department to write rules stopping companies from raising wholesale gasoline prices more than once every 24 hours, and would have capped the profits of oil companies that sell gasoline wholesale at their average profits from 2001 through 2005, effective through the end of fiscal year 2006. It also directed federal agencies to propose actions to cut U.S. oil demand by at least one million barrels per day by 2013, and ordered the Federal Trade Commission to investigate whether companies price-gouged gasoline customers after Hurricane Katrina and whether market consolidation drove prices up [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Motorists and other gasoline consumers, who would get relief from rapid price increases at the wholesale level and an official accounting of whether post-Katrina price hikes were gouging; the country broadly, through reduced dependence on foreign oil [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bars companies from raising wholesale gasoline prices more than once every 24 hours, limiting the speed of price spikes that reach the pump [S2][S3].
Caps wholesale gasoline sellers' profits at their FY2001-FY2005 average through the end of FY2006, clawing back windfall profits from the post-Katrina price surge [S2][S3].

Orders the FTC to investigate whether wholesale and retail gasoline price gouging occurred after Hurricane Katrina, and whether market consolidation raised consumer prices, with recommendations for enforcement [S2][S3].
Directs federal agencies to propose actions cutting U.S. oil demand by at least one million barrels per day versus projected 2013 demand, reducing waste and reliance on foreign oil [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies selling gasoline on the wholesale market, whose profits would be capped at their five-year average through fiscal 2006, and companies that would face restrictions on how often they can raise wholesale prices [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Wholesale gasoline sellers and oil companies

drawbacks.text: Capping profits at a historical average is a blunt tool: it could discourage refiners from producing more gasoline precisely when supply was tight after Hurricane Katrina, potentially worsening shortages [S3].

Limiting wholesale price changes to once every 24 hours interferes with prices that normally adjust continuously in a volatile commodity market, which could disconnect wholesale prices from actual supply costs [S3].
The one-million-barrel-per-day conservation mandate sets a numeric target but only requires agencies to 'propose' actions, leaving the actual measures unspecified and their costs unknown [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers facing a sudden, post-Katrina price spike, the profit cap and price-hike limit offered direct, immediate relief, and the FTC investigation promised an official answer on gouging. The cost is real but temporary: the profit cap was to expire after fiscal 2006, and the main risk is that interference with wholesale pricing could discourage supply during an emergency. It was a crisis-response bill, not a durable energy policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced the day after Labor Day 2005, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended with no hearing and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on September 2, 2005, in the immediate aftermath of Hurricane Katrina, which had disrupted Gulf Coast refining and sent gasoline prices sharply higher [S1][S3].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].

On September 19, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it remained; the committee never reported it and the full House never voted on it before the 109th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies selling gasoline wholesale kept the post-Katrina windfall profits the bill would have clawed back, and no FTC investigation into consolidation-driven pricing was compelled by this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale gasoline sellers kept windfall profits

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap oil company profits, restrict wholesale gasoline price hikes, and order a post-Katrina price-gouging investigation.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Joe Barton, R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill, never scheduling a hearing or markup; it was referred to subcommittee on September 19, 2005, and died there.

against.name: Oil and gasoline wholesale industry
against.role: Industry affected by profit cap and price-hike limits
against.what_they_did: The bill's profit caps and price restrictions targeted wholesale gasoline sellers; industry opposition to windfall-profits caps was the principal obstacle such measures faced in the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat and the bill drew zero cosponsors of either party; it died in a committee chaired by a Republican without ever reaching the floor [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Oil refiners and wholesale gasoline sellers
industries.note: The bill would cap their profits at a five-year average through fiscal 2006 and limit how often they could raise wholesale prices, directly clawing back post-Katrina windfall gains. Consumers' savings on gasoline would have come out of these companies' margins [S2][S3].

Retailers were subjects of the proposed FTC gouging investigation and could face enforcement if gouging was found, but many retail stations operate on thin margins and price increases largely originate upstream [S2][S3].
A mandated one-million-barrel-per-day reduction in U.S. oil demand by 2013 would cut import demand, and the bill frames this as decreasing reliance on foreign oil [S2][S3].
